de: Alexander Fleming noticed a mould killing bacteria on a contaminated plate. Florey and Chain developed it into a usable drug and mass production began during the Second World War. Before antibiotics, a scratch from a rose thorn or an infected tooth could kill a healthy adult.

blocks.t: Antibiotics are credited with saving hundreds of millions of lives. Antimicrobial resistance now threatens to reverse part of that gain, killing an estimated 1.3 million people a year directly.
Within one lifetime, infections that routinely killed children became a week of tablets. Also a warning: this gift is being spent faster than it is being replaced.

meta: A Breakthrough · Mexico and South Asia
de: Norman Borlaug, an agronomist and a devout Christian who said he was doing the Lord's work in feeding the hungry, bred high-yield disease-resistant wheat in Mexico and brought it to India and Pakistan in the 1960s, when mass famine was widely predicted there.

blocks.t: India went from importing grain to self-sufficiency within a decade. Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 and is often credited with saving up to a billion lives — more than any other person in history. Critics note the increased dependence on fertilizer, irrigation, and monoculture.
The man who may have saved a billion lives is not on any coin or stamp most children would recognize. He spent his life in wheat fields. Ask a child if they can name him, then tell them what he did.

t: A Spoon of Salt and Sugar
de: Researchers in Dhaka and Kolkata established that a simple solution of clean water, salt and sugar could rehydrate a child dying of diarrhoeal disease as effectively as intravenous fluids, at almost no cost. It was deployed at scale in refugee camps during the 1971 Bangladesh war.

blocks.t: Oral rehydration therapy has been credited with saving tens of millions of children's lives. The Lancet called it potentially the most important medical advance of the twentieth century. Diarrhoeal deaths in children have fallen by more than two-thirds since 1990.
The single most effective child-saving intervention in modern history costs a few cents and can be mixed by a mother at a kitchen table. Not every solution requires a laboratory.

de: The World Health Assembly declared smallpox eradicated after a global campaign of surveillance and ring vaccination. The last natural case was Ali Maow Maalin, a hospital cook in Somalia, in 1977. Smallpox had killed an estimated 300 million people in the twentieth century alone.

blocks.t: It remains the only human disease ever deliberately eradicated. Rinderpest, a cattle disease, was eradicated in 2011. Polio has been reduced by over 99 percent and survives in a handful of areas.

Humanity, cooperating across every ideological divide of the Cold War, permanently removed one of its greatest killers from the earth. The Soviet Union and the United States funded it together at the height of their hostility. It can be done.

de: In 1800, roughly 43 percent of the world's children died before their fifth birthday. By 1990 the global under-five mortality rate was about 93 per 1,000 live births. Today it is around 37 per 1,000 — a fall of roughly 60 percent in a single generation.

blocks.t: That is on the order of fifteen thousand fewer children dying every day than would have died at 1990 rates. The main drivers were vaccination, oral rehydration, bed nets, clean water, better nutrition, and skilled birth attendance.

This is the number that should be on the front page every day and never is. For most of history, half the children born did not live to five. Almost every mother buried a child. That is no longer true, and it changed within living memory.

de: In 1820 roughly one person in ten over fifteen could read. By 1930 it was about one in three. Today global literacy stands at approximately 87 percent, and youth literacy is higher still. Female literacy, historically far behind, has closed most of the gap in most regions.

blocks.t: Economic historians Becker and Woessmann found that Protestant regions of nineteenth-century Prussia had measurably higher literacy and incomes, and argue the mechanism was religious: Protestants were expected to read scripture for themselves.

The insistence that ordinary people must read the word of Heavenly Father for themselves is one of the documented origins of mass literacy. Teaching a child to read scripture at bedtime sits inside a very old and very consequential tradition.

de: In 1900 global average life expectancy at birth was around 32 years. By 2021 it had more than doubled to roughly 71 years. Life expectancy has more than doubled in every world region — not only in rich countries.

blocks.t: The gain is not only from fewer child deaths; survival improved at every age. A person today can expect to know their grandchildren, which for most of history was uncommon.
Three or four generations ago, most people never met a grandparent. The multigenerational family — the thing your books assume — is in historical terms a very recent gift.

t: Extreme Poverty Falls Below Ten Percent
de: Roughly 90 percent of the world lived in extreme poverty in 1820. About half did in 1950. More than a third still did in 1990. By 2019 it had fallen below 10 percent. Economist Michail Moatsos notes it took 136 years for the rate to fall below 50 percent, then 45 more years to halve again by 2001, then only 13 years to halve again by 2014.

blocks.t: The United Nations goal of halving 1990 poverty by 2015 was met five years early. The largest single contributors were China and India, after each moved toward secure property, open trade, and market pricing.

More people left extreme poverty in the last forty years than in the previous forty centuries. Almost no one knows this. Surveys repeatedly find that most people in rich countries believe global poverty has been rising.

de: Roughly 700 million people still live in extreme poverty. In Sub-Saharan Africa the share living in extreme poverty fell, but the total number rose, because population grew faster than incomes. Almost 40 percent of the region lives in extreme poverty.

blocks.t: World Bank projections suggest the long decline in global extreme poverty may be ending. On current growth rates, close to one billion people could remain in extreme poverty for decades, and the number in 2040 may be higher than today, because most of the remaining poor live in countries with stagnant economies or active conflict.

Do not close this layer on a victory lap. The escape was real and it is stalling. Where it stalled is where war, corruption, and insecure property remain — which is the argument of every other layer on this timeline, stated in reverse.

de: Historians and economists disagree about the relative weight of causes, but the recurring ingredients are: secure property and the ability to keep the fruit of your work; open exchange of goods and ideas; the scientific method; mass literacy; public sanitation; and political stability under predictable law.

blocks.t: No region has escaped mass poverty while lacking most of these. Several have escaped it in a single generation once they were in place — South Korea, Taiwan, Ireland, Poland, and to a large degree China and India.

This is the layer that answers the objection that faith and freedom talk is abstract. It is not abstract. It is the difference between a mother burying half her children and a mother watching all of them learn to read. That is the whole argument, measured.

de: Debt bondage and captive slavery appear in Sumer, Babylon, Egypt, China, India, Greece, and Rome, and independently in the Americas, Africa, and the Pacific. Hammurabi's code regulates the sale and return of slaves. No major ancient civilization is known to have existed without some form of it.

blocks.t: For roughly five thousand years, virtually no one on earth argued that slavery as such was wrong. Aristotle defended it as natural. The question debated was who could rightly be enslaved, not whether anyone could.

Start here, because it is the part people forget. Slavery was not a Western invention or an African one. It was the human default on every continent. What needs explaining is not why it existed but why it ever stopped.

de: Heavenly Father delivered Israel from slavery in Egypt. The law given afterward repeatedly grounds its ethics in that memory: remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt. Hebrew servitude was limited to six years, runaway slaves were not to be returned to their masters, and killing a slave was punishable.

blocks.t: The Exodus became the founding story of a people and, three thousand years later, the central metaphor of the abolitionist movement and of the American civil rights movement. Go Down Moses was sung by enslaved people in the American South.

The oldest liberation story on earth is scripture, and it was still being sung by people in chains thirty-three centuries later. That is why every entry below about faith and abolition traces back to this one.

t: Slave Societies of Greece and Rome
de: At its height perhaps a third of the population of Roman Italy was enslaved. Slaves worked mines, farms, households, and arenas. Roman law classed them as property that could be tortured for evidence and killed at the owner's discretion for much of the Republic.

blocks.t: Roman slavery was not racial — captives came from Gaul, Britain, Germany, Greece, and Africa alike. It collapsed slowly with the empire and shifted into serfdom rather than ending.
The greatest legal minds of the ancient world built the most sophisticated law code before modern times, and never seriously questioned owning people. Brilliance is not the same as moral clarity.

de: Paul sent the runaway slave Onesimus back to his owner Philemon, but asked Philemon to receive him not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved. Elsewhere Paul wrote that in Christ there is neither bond nor free, while also instructing servants to obey their masters.

blocks.t: These passages were quoted on both sides of the abolition debate for eighteen centuries. Defenders of slavery cited the instruction to obey. Abolitionists cited the brotherhood. Both were reading the same letters.

Marked mixed, honestly. Scripture did not end slavery on contact — it took eighteen hundred years. But the seed planted here, that a slave is a brother, is what eventually made the institution impossible to defend among people who took the text seriously.

t: The Trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean Trades
meta: Human Bondage · Sahara, Red Sea, Indian Ocean
de: Slave trades across the Sahara, the Red Sea, and the Indian Ocean operated for well over a thousand years, longer than the Atlantic trade. Historians estimate totals broadly comparable to the Atlantic trade, though records are far sparser. Male captives were frequently castrated, and the trades drew on East and West Africa, the Caucasus, and Slavic Europe — the word slave derives from Slav.

blocks.t: These trades ran from roughly the seventh century into the twentieth. Saudi Arabia and Yemen did not formally abolish slavery until 1962, Mauritania not until 1981, and Mauritania did not criminalize it until 2007.

Included because a timeline that discusses only the Atlantic trade is not telling the truth. Slavery was a global system with many participants, and the last legal abolitions happened within living memory.

meta: Human Bondage · West Africa to the Americas
de: Portuguese ships began carrying African captives to Europe in 1444, and to the Americas from 1501. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, built from roughly 36,000 documented voyages, estimates 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard and 10.7 million survived to disembark. By nation: Portugal 5.8 million, Britain 3.3 million, France 1.4 million, Spain 1.1 million, the Netherlands 554,000, the United States 305,000.

blocks.t: Approximately 1.8 million people died during the Middle Passage. Captives were sold by African kingdoms as well as captured directly; the trade required suppliers as well as buyers. Entire regions of West Africa were depopulated and destabilized for generations.

1.8 million people died in the crossing alone — more than the entire population of many nations at the time. Every one of them had a mother. This is the single largest forced separation of families in recorded history.

meta: Abolition Driven by Faith · Germantown, Pennsylvania
de: Four Quakers in Germantown wrote the first known formal protest against slavery in the American colonies. Their argument was simple and religious: there is a saying, that we shall doe to all men like as we will be done our selves; making no difference of what generation, descent or colour they are.

blocks.t: The petition was passed up the Quaker hierarchy and quietly shelved. But Quakers kept pressing, and by 1776 the Society of Friends had barred slaveholding among its own members — the first organization of any kind to do so.

The first written argument against slavery in America was the Golden Rule, applied without exception. Four ordinary people wrote it, it was ignored, and it won anyway — eighty-eight years later inside their own church, and two centuries later across the world.

meta: Abolition Driven by Faith · London, England
de: James Somerset, an enslaved man brought to England, escaped and was recaptured. Granville Sharp, an evangelical Anglican, funded his case. Lord Mansfield ruled that slavery was so odious that nothing can be suffered to support it but positive law, and ordered Somerset discharged.

blocks.t: The ruling was widely understood to mean slavery could not exist on English soil. It became a rallying point for the abolition movement and was cited by enslaved people in America who reached free jurisdictions.
One man, Granville Sharp, spent his own money on one stranger's freedom because he believed it was required of him. That single case cracked the legal foundation of an empire's slave system.

meta: Abolition Driven by Faith · Clapham, London
de: William Wilberforce, an evangelical Member of Parliament, recorded in 1787 that God Almighty has set before me two great objects, the suppression of the slave trade and the reformation of manners. He worked with the Clapham Sect — a group of evangelical Anglicans including Sharp, Thomas Clarkson, Hannah More, and Olaudah Equiano, a formerly enslaved man whose published narrative moved the British public.

blocks.t: Wilberforce introduced abolition bills and lost, repeatedly, for eighteen years. Parliament abolished the slave trade in 1807. The Slavery Abolition Act passed in 1833, three days before Wilberforce died. Roughly 800,000 people were freed across the British Caribbean by 1838.

Eighteen years of losing. This is the clearest case in modern history of religious conviction driving a moral revolution against overwhelming economic interest — and it required a lifetime, not a moment.

de: Having abolished its own trade, Britain deployed the Royal Navy to stop everyone else's. The West Africa Squadron patrolled the coast for sixty years, at times using a fifth of the entire navy, and Britain paid other nations to accept inspection treaties.

blocks.t: Between 1820 and 1870 the squadron seized over 1,500 ships and freed roughly 150,000 Africans. Around 17,000 British sailors died, mostly of disease. Britain spent an estimated 1.8 percent of national income annually on suppression for decades.

The nation that had shipped 3.3 million people into slavery then spent sixty years and thousands of its own lives trying to stop the trade. Repentance at national scale is possible, it is expensive, and it does not undo what came before.

meta: Complex Legacy · Britain and the Caribbean
de: The Slavery Abolition Act freed roughly 800,000 people, but Parliament voted 20 million pounds in compensation — around 40 percent of the national budget — to the slave owners for their lost property. The formerly enslaved received nothing, and were required to serve a further period of unpaid apprenticeship until 1838.

blocks.t: The British government finished repaying the loan taken out to fund that compensation in 2015. Taxpayers, including descendants of enslaved people, were servicing that debt for 182 years.

Marked mixed because the abolition was real and the injustice inside it was also real. The people freed were made to work unpaid for five more years while their former owners were paid. Doing the right thing badly is still worth doing, and it still leaves a debt.

de: American churches split over slavery. The Southern Baptist Convention was founded in 1845 specifically so that slaveholders could serve as missionaries. Methodists and Presbyterians divided similarly. Southern clergy defended slavery from scripture; Northern abolitionists attacked it from the same scripture. Frederick Douglass distinguished sharply between the Christianity of Christ and the slaveholding religion of this land.

blocks.t: The Southern Baptist Convention formally apologized in 1995, on its 150th anniversary, repudiating its founding and asking forgiveness of African Americans. Other denominations issued similar apologies.

This entry is uncomfortable and belongs here. The same book was used to justify the chain and to break it. What decided the reading was not the text but whether the reader was profiting from the answer.

t: Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad
meta: Abolition Driven by Faith · Maryland to the North
de: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery in 1849 and then returned to the South roughly thirteen times, personally leading about seventy people to freedom. She described her guidance as direct answers to prayer and never lost a passenger. The wider Underground Railroad was staffed heavily by Quakers, free Black communities, and African Methodist Episcopal congregations.

blocks.t: Estimates suggest the network helped tens of thousands escape. Tubman later served as a scout and spy for the Union Army and led the Combahee Ferry raid that freed more than 700 people in a single night.
She was already free. She went back thirteen times. Whatever else faith does, it is what sends people back into danger for strangers who share nothing with them but a Father.

de: Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States. It followed a war that killed roughly 620,000 to 750,000 Americans — more than every other American war combined.

blocks.t: Roughly four million people were freed. Formerly enslaved people immediately sought out spouses and children sold away, formalized marriages by the tens of thousands, and founded schools and churches. The exception clause for convicted prisoners was later exploited through convict leasing.
America paid for this with more of its own dead than any other cause in its history. And the first thing the freed did with their freedom was look for their families.

t: Brazil, the Last in the Americas
meta: Freedom Won · Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
de: Brazil received roughly 40 percent of all Africans brought to the Americas — more than any other country, about ten times the number brought to the United States. The Golden Law abolished slavery without compensation to owners, making Brazil the last country in the Western Hemisphere to end it.

blocks.t: Around 700,000 people were freed. No land, compensation, or transition support was provided, and the monarchy fell the following year partly as a result of planter anger.

Four hundred years after it began in the Americas, it ended. The scale correction matters: most people assume the United States was the center of the Atlantic trade. It received about 2.4 percent of it.

de: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that no one shall be held in slavery or servitude, and that slavery and the slave trade shall be prohibited in all their forms. For the first time, the prohibition was declared universal rather than national.

blocks.t: Mauritania became the last country on earth to abolish slavery legally, in 1981, and did not make it a criminal offence until 2007. Slavery is now illegal in every country in the world.
It took humanity roughly five thousand years to write that sentence down and mean it everywhere. It has been the law of the whole world for less than eighty years.

de: The Global Slavery Index and the International Labour Organization estimate roughly 50 million people live in modern slavery — about 28 million in forced labour and 22 million in forced marriage. It includes debt bondage in South Asian brick kilns and agriculture, forced labour in fishing and manufacturing supply chains, state-imposed labour, and sex trafficking. Roughly one in four is a child.

blocks.t: That is more people in bondage than at any previous point in history in absolute terms, though a far smaller share of a much larger world population. It is illegal everywhere and happens everywhere, including in wealthy countries.

Do not end this layer feeling that it is over. There are more people enslaved today than were carried across the Atlantic in three and a half centuries. The difference is that now every one of them is being held illegally — which means it can be found, and it can be stopped.

de: For roughly five millennia, on every continent, virtually no one argued slavery as such was wrong. Within about a century and a half — roughly 1780 to 1900 — it went from universal and respectable to universally condemned. Historians differ on the causes, weighing economic change, Enlightenment thought, and the resistance of enslaved people themselves, which was constant and essential.

blocks.t: What is not seriously disputed is that the organized abolition movements in Britain and America were overwhelmingly led and staffed by religious people acting on religious conviction: Quakers, evangelical Anglicans, Methodists, and the Black church.

Here is the honest version of the claim. Faith did not end slavery quickly — it took eighteen centuries, and believers were on both sides. But when the thing finally broke, the people doing the breaking were mostly acting on a conviction that every person is a child of Heavenly Father. Free societies made the argument possible. Faith supplied the reason. Neither one did it alone.

meta: Freedom to Own and Build · Babylon
de: Babylon published 282 laws on a stone pillar set in public where any citizen could read them. Many concern property: contracts, wages, rent, inheritance, liability for shoddy building. The point was not that the laws were gentle — many were harsh — but that they were written down and the same for everyone who could read them.

blocks.t: Written, public, predictable law made long-distance trade and lending possible. Babylon became the commercial center of the ancient world.
Prosperity begins with a rule you can read in advance. Where the law is whatever the powerful say it is today, no one plants, builds, or lends.

meta: Freedom to Own and Build · Israel
de: Leviticus 25 established that every family held land as an inheritance that could not be permanently sold. Every seventh year debts were released and land rested. Every fiftieth year — the Jubilee — land returned to the family that held it, and Israelites in debt-servitude went free. Gleaning laws required harvesters to leave the edges of the field for the poor.

blocks.t: Scholars debate how consistently Jubilee was observed. What is not debated is the principle: property was real and protected, and also periodically reset so that debt could not permanently destroy a family line.

Heavenly Father gave a property system that protected ownership and refused to let one bad generation disinherit all the ones after it. Both halves matter. Ownership without mercy grinds families down; mercy without ownership removes the reason to build.

meta: Freedom to Own and Build · Runnymede, England
de: English barons forced King John to accept that no free man could be seized or dispossessed except by lawful judgment of his peers and the law of the land, and that the crown could not levy certain taxes without consent.

blocks.t: The principle that the sovereign is under the law, and cannot simply take what he wants, became the root of English common law and eventually of American constitutional protection of property.
The first great charter of liberty in the English-speaking world was largely about property. People do not build what a king can seize on a whim.

meta: Freedom to Own and Build · Amsterdam, Dutch Republic
de: The Dutch East India Company issued tradable shares to the public and the Amsterdam exchange was founded to trade them — the first modern capital market. The Dutch Republic also offered unusual religious toleration, drawing in Sephardic Jews expelled from Iberia and Huguenots fleeing France.

blocks.t: A small, waterlogged country with almost no natural resources became the richest per person in Europe for roughly a century, and a center of printing, science, and art.

The Dutch case joins both of your layers. They took in the people other nations expelled for their faith, and gave them secure property and tradable capital. Toleration and ownership compounded together.

meta: Freedom to Own and Build · London, England
de: John Locke argued in the Second Treatise that a person owns himself and therefore owns what he mixes his labour with, that government exists chiefly to protect life, liberty and property, and that a government which seizes property without consent forfeits its legitimacy.

blocks.t: Locke's formulation runs almost verbatim into the American Declaration of Independence, and property protection into the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments.
Self-ownership is the hinge. If you own yourself, you own your work. If someone else owns your work, they own you. Every entry below turns on that sentence.

meta: Freedom to Own and Build · Edinburgh, Scotland
de: Adam Smith, a professor of moral philosophy, argued that a butcher, brewer and baker serve us not from benevolence but from regard to their own interest, and that voluntary exchange under just laws makes both parties better off. He also warned repeatedly against merchants conspiring against the public and against masters combining to hold down wages.

blocks.t: Published the same year as the Declaration of Independence. Nations that adopted broadly market economies with secure property saw sustained growth in living standards for the first time in human history.

Smith is routinely quoted by people who have not read him. He wrote The Theory of Moral Sentiments first and thought markets only worked inside a moral community. Free exchange without honesty is just a faster way to cheat.

de: Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto, summarizing their programme in a single sentence: abolition of private property. It also called for abolition of inheritance and of the family in its existing form, and described religion as an instrument of oppression.

blocks.t: Within seventy years a state built on this programme controlled Russia. Within a century roughly a third of humanity lived under governments founded on it. The next four entries are what followed.

Included as the hinge of this layer. This is one of the very few ideas in history that was proposed in writing, implemented at scale in many countries, and can now be assessed against its own stated goals.

meta: Ownership Taken Away · Ukraine and Soviet Union
de: The Soviet state abolished private farming, seized land and livestock into collective farms, and deported or executed peasants labelled kulaks for owning slightly more than their neighbours. Grain quotas were enforced while famine spread, and peasants were forbidden to leave.

blocks.t: Roughly 3.5 to 5 million died in Ukraine in 1932-33, with millions more across Kazakhstan and Russia. Kazakhstan lost an estimated third of its population. Soviet agriculture never recovered its pre-collectivization productivity and the USSR, sitting on some of the best farmland on earth, became a net grain importer.
The most fertile soil in Europe produced mass starvation within four years of the farmers losing title to it. Not because the land changed. Because the ownership did.

de: China abolished private plots, collectivized roughly 550 million peasants into communes, banned private cooking in favour of communal kitchens, and required backyard steel furnaces that consumed farm tools and produced unusable metal. Local officials reported inflated harvests upward, and quotas were set against the false numbers.

blocks.t: Historians estimate 15 to 45 million deaths from famine between 1959 and 1961, among the deadliest famines in recorded history. It ended when private plots and material incentives were quietly restored.

Two mechanisms, both visible here. Remove ownership and people stop producing. Remove free speech and no one can report that the harvest failed. Economic freedom and freedom of conscience fail together.

de: Germany was divided between a market economy with private property in the west and a centrally planned economy with state ownership in the east. Same language, same history, same faith traditions, same people — often the same families split across the line.

blocks.t: By 1989 West German GDP per capita was roughly double the East's, and East German industry was so far behind that much of it could not compete after reunification. The Berlin Wall was built in 1961 because roughly 2.7 million people had already left east to west; almost no one moved the other way.
When a wall has to be built to keep people in rather than out, the experiment has already returned its verdict. People vote with their feet before they vote with anything else.

meta: A Natural Experiment · The 38th parallel, Korea
de: Korea was divided along the 38th parallel. Same people, same language, same 5,000-year history, similar starting poverty — in 1960 South Korea's GDP per capita was about 1,000 dollars, poorer than much of sub-Saharan Africa. The north kept state ownership of nearly everything; the south moved toward private property, contract enforcement and open trade.

blocks.t: Today South Korea's GDP per capita is roughly 36,000 dollars against North Korea's 1,300 — about a 27-fold gap, and roughly 36-fold adjusted for purchasing power. On the Heritage Index of Economic Freedom, South Korea scores 73.7 and ranks 24th of 197. North Korea scores 3.1 and ranks 197th of 197 — last on earth. Satellite photographs at night show the south blazing with light and the north almost entirely dark.

This is the closest thing social science has to a controlled experiment on a whole nation. Identical people, identical land, identical culture, identical faith background. One variable changed. You can see the result from space.

t: Eighteen Farmers Sign a Secret Contract
meta: Freedom to Own and Build · Xiaogang, Anhui, China
de: Eighteen farmers in the starving village of Xiaogang secretly agreed in writing to divide the commune land into family plots, meet the state quota, and keep whatever they grew beyond it. The document was a capital crime; they pledged to raise each other's children if they were executed. Deng Xiaoping's reforms shortly afterward legalized the practice nationwide.

blocks.t: Xiaogang's harvest the following year exceeded the previous five years combined. Scaled nationally, China's reforms are credited with lifting roughly 800 million people out of extreme poverty — the largest and fastest reduction in poverty in human history.

Eighteen illiterate farmers risking execution for the right to keep what they grew produced more food in one year than the commune had in five. They did not need a new theory. They needed to own the result of their own work.

meta: Freedom to Own and Build · New Delhi, India
de: Facing a balance of payments crisis, India dismantled the Licence Raj — a system in which starting or expanding a business required government permits — cut tariffs, and opened to foreign investment.

blocks.t: Indian growth accelerated sharply. Extreme poverty in India fell from roughly half the population in the early 1990s to a small fraction today, moving hundreds of millions of people out of it.
India did not change its religion, its culture, or its climate in 1991. It changed the rules about who may start a business without asking permission.

meta: Freedom to Own and Build · Lima, Peru
de: Economist Hernando de Soto documented that the poor are not poor because they own nothing, but because what they own is not legally recognized. His teams found that formally registering a small business in Peru took roughly 300 days of full-time effort. He estimated the value of untitled property held by the world's poor at some 9.3 trillion dollars — dead capital that cannot be used as collateral, sold securely, or inherited.

blocks.t: Land titling programmes followed in Peru, Thailand, Rwanda and elsewhere, with studies generally finding increased investment, greater access to credit, and more household labour supply once title was secure.

A family living in a house they cannot prove they own cannot borrow against it to start a business or send a child to school. Recognizing what poor families already have is one of the cheapest and most powerful policies available.

de: Venezuela nationalized oil, steel, cement, telecoms, farmland and thousands of businesses, imposed price controls, and expropriated foreign and domestic firms, while sitting on the largest proven oil reserves in the world.

blocks.t: Output collapsed, hyperinflation followed, and food and medicine became scarce. Roughly 7.7 million Venezuelans have left the country — among the largest displacement crises on earth, comparable to Syria's.
Included because it is recent and unambiguous. The country with the most oil on earth produced a refugee crisis. Natural wealth does not protect a nation whose people cannot securely own anything.

t: Married Women Gain the Right to Own
meta: Freedom to Own and Build · Britain and the United States
de: Under coverture, a married woman's legal identity merged into her husband's: she could not own property, sign contracts, or keep her own wages. Mississippi passed the first Married Women's Property Act in 1839; Britain followed in 1870 and 1882, and most American states by 1900.

blocks.t: Modern research on developing countries consistently finds that when women hold secure property and income, more household spending goes to children's food, health and schooling. Strengthening women's property rights is now a standard development intervention.
For most of history, half of humanity could not legally own the results of their own work. When that changed, the first thing it changed was what children ate.

de: The Homestead Act granted 160 acres to any citizen or intending citizen, including women and later freed slaves, who would live on and improve the land for five years. Roughly 1.6 million claims were eventually patented, covering about ten percent of U.S. land.

blocks.t: It created a large class of owner-occupier farming families across the American interior. It also distributed land taken from Native nations, and the same era saw treaties broken and tribes removed — and later, under the Dawes Act, Native communal landholding forcibly broken up.

Marked mixed because both are true and a serious timeline says so. Widespread family ownership genuinely built the American middle class. It was carried out on land taken from families who had it first.

de: Indexes of economic freedom measure property rights, contract enforcement, regulatory burden, trade openness and sound money. Countries in the top quartile consistently show far higher income per person, longer life expectancy, and lower rates of extreme poverty than those in the bottom quartile.

blocks.t: The correlation is one of the more robust findings in comparative economics. Causation is debated, and rich countries plainly find good institutions easier to maintain — but no country has ever become wealthy while abolishing private ownership, and several have become poor doing it.

An honest caution to close on: economic freedom is necessary but not sufficient. It does not by itself produce honesty, generosity, or strong families. It gives people the room to build. What they build in that room is decided by what they believe.

de: Residue analysis of pottery jars at Jiahu identified a fermented beverage of rice, honey, and fruit — the earliest chemically confirmed alcoholic drink. Beer and wine appear independently in Sumer and Egypt within a few thousand years, usually tied to temple ritual and daily rations.

blocks.t: Alcohol became embedded in nearly every civilization on earth, simultaneously as a sacrament, a medicine, a wage, and a source of ruin. Genesis 9 records Noah planting a vineyard and the harm that followed within his own family.
The very first recorded story of alcohol in scripture is a story about what it did to a family. That pattern has not changed in nine thousand years.

de: Sumerian tablets refer to the opium poppy as hul gil, commonly translated as the joy plant. Cultivation spread to Assyria, Egypt, and Greece, where opium was used for pain, sleep, and ritual.

blocks.t: Opium remained the most effective painkiller available to humanity for the next five thousand years, and the most reliable source of addiction. Every later opioid — morphine, heroin, oxycodone, fentanyl — descends from this plant or imitates it.
The oldest painkiller and the oldest addiction are the same plant. Humanity has never solved the problem of a substance that relieves suffering and creates it.

de: Andean peoples chewed coca leaf for altitude, hunger, and endurance, and used it ceremonially. In leaf form it is a mild stimulant, chemically far removed from concentrated cocaine, which would not be isolated until 1860.

blocks.t: Traditional coca use persisted for millennia without producing the social devastation associated with cocaine. The Spanish later taxed coca and issued it to forced laborers in the silver mines of Potosi to extend working hours.
Concentration is what turns a plant into a weapon. The same leaf that sustained Andean farmers for five thousand years became, once refined, one of the most destructive commodities on earth.

de: Columbus recorded Taino people smoking dried leaves. Tobacco reached Europe within a generation and became a global commodity. Jamestown survived economically because of tobacco, which required intensive labor.

blocks.t: Tobacco demand drove the expansion of chattel slavery in the American South. It later became the deadliest consumer product in history, killing an estimated eight million people a year worldwide today according to the World Health Organization.

Tobacco built colonies, funded slavery, and now kills more people annually than any illegal drug on this layer combined. The most lethal drug in history has been legal almost everywhere the entire time.

de: Cheap unlicensed gin flooded London after Parliament deregulated distilling. At the peak, consumption was estimated near two pints per person per week across the whole population, including children. Hogarth's 1751 print Gin Lane depicted a drunken mother letting her infant fall — the era's defining image.

blocks.t: Burials exceeded baptisms in London for much of the period. Contemporary observers blamed gin for child neglect, abandonment, and infant mortality. The Gin Act of 1751 raised duties and restricted sales to licensed premises, and consumption fell sharply over the following decade.

The first mass drug epidemic of the modern era was legal, taxed, and marketed — and the harm was measured first in what happened to children. It was also solved, which matters: policy changed the outcome within a decade.

meta: A Response That Helped · Kirtland, Ohio
de: Joseph Smith received the revelation recorded as Doctrine and Covenants 89, counseling against wine and strong drink, tobacco, and hot drinks. It was given at a time when tobacco use was near universal among American men and the medical consensus held tobacco to be harmless or beneficial.

blocks.t: For over a century the counsel had no scientific support. The first major studies linking smoking to lung cancer appeared in the 1950s; the U.S. Surgeon General's report came in 1964 — 131 years later. Latter-day Saint populations have been repeatedly documented with markedly lower rates of lung cancer, cardiovascular disease, and substance use disorder.

A revelation given in 1833 anticipated by more than a century what medicine would confirm in 1964. Whatever else it is, it is one of the most testable prophetic claims in the Restoration, and the test has run.

meta: State or Cartel Power · Canton and coastal China
de: Britain ran a deliberate state-backed trade deficit correction by selling Indian-grown opium into China. When Commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed 1,200 tons of confiscated opium at Humen in 1839, Britain went to war to keep the trade open, and again in 1856. China lost both wars.

blocks.t: Opium was legalized by treaty. By the early twentieth century tens of millions of Chinese were addicted. China ceded Hong Kong and signed the treaties it remembers as the Century of Humiliation, a grievance that still shapes Chinese foreign policy today.
The most powerful nation on earth fought two wars for the right to sell an addictive drug to someone else's children. When a government profits from addiction, it will defend that profit with force.

de: Morphine was isolated from opium in 1804 and mass-produced after the hypodermic syringe arrived in 1853, creating widespread addiction among wounded soldiers. In 1898 Bayer marketed diacetylmorphine under the brand name Heroin as a non-addictive cough remedy and morphine substitute, sold over the counter and advertised for children.

blocks.t: Heroin proved substantially more addictive than morphine. Bayer withdrew it in 1913. The United States restricted opiates through the Harrison Narcotics Act in 1914 and banned heroin outright in 1924.
Heroin was invented by a respected pharmaceutical company, tested, approved, advertised as safe, and given to children. Ninety-eight years later the same thing happened again with OxyContin.

de: The Eighteenth Amendment banned the manufacture and sale of alcohol, driven substantially by the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, whose core argument was the protection of wives and children from drunken husbands.

blocks.t: Alcohol consumption fell by an estimated 30 to 50 percent and cirrhosis deaths dropped sharply. It also created organized crime on a national scale, funding Al Capone and the modern American mafia. It was repealed in 1933.

The honest verdict is genuinely mixed and worth sitting with. Prohibition measurably reduced drinking and the harm to families that motivated it. It also built the criminal infrastructure that later distributed heroin and cocaine. Both are true.

de: The new communist government launched a mass campaign against opium: forced treatment for millions of users, execution or imprisonment of dealers, and destruction of poppy fields, conducted alongside mass mobilization and public denunciation.

blocks.t: Historians generally agree that China effectively eliminated a national addiction crisis involving tens of millions of people within roughly three years — one of the few complete reversals of a mass epidemic on record. It was achieved by methods no free society could or should replicate.

Included because it complicates the story rather than simplifying it. Total state coercion did end the epidemic, at a cost in executions and forced internment that a free country cannot pay. Effectiveness is not the only question worth asking.

meta: A Response That Helped · Washington D.C.
de: President Nixon named drug abuse public enemy number one and created the framework that became the DEA. Enforcement spending expanded steadily for five decades, and the U.S. prison population grew from roughly 200,000 in 1970 to over 1.5 million by 2010, with drug offenses a major driver.

blocks.t: Illegal drug prices generally fell and purity generally rose over the same period, the opposite of the intended effect. Incarceration removed large numbers of parents — disproportionately fathers, and disproportionately from Black and Hispanic communities — from their households.

A policy designed to protect families removed millions of parents from homes while the drugs became cheaper and stronger. Intentions and outcomes are different things, and only outcomes can be measured.

de: Crack, a smokable and inexpensive form of cocaine, spread rapidly through American cities. Sentencing law treated crack roughly one hundred times more severely than powder cocaine by weight, a disparity Congress reduced only in 2010.

blocks.t: Homicide rates among young Black men roughly doubled. Foster care caseloads rose sharply as parents were incarcerated or lost custody. Research following the so-called crack baby panic later found the predicted birth defects were substantially overstated, while the damage from family separation and poverty was very real.
Two lessons at once. The drug did enormous harm to families. And the moral panic around it produced sentencing law that did additional harm, to the same families, for another twenty-six years.

de: Purdue Pharma launched OxyContin with marketing claiming addiction risk was under one percent. Sales representatives were sent to general practitioners with no pain-management training. Purdue pleaded guilty to federal criminal charges in 2007 and again in 2020.

blocks.t: Roughly 645,000 Americans died of opioid overdose between 1999 and 2021. Purdue and the Sackler family agreed to settlements exceeding six billion dollars. Overdose became the leading cause of death for Americans aged 18 to 44. Hundreds of thousands of children entered kinship or foster care because of parental opioid use.

This did not come from a cartel or a street corner. It came from a licensed pharmaceutical company, prescribed by licensed doctors, approved by federal regulators. The most destructive drug epidemic in American history was, at its origin, entirely legal.

de: President Calderon deployed the military against the cartels in December 2006. The conflict fragmented the large cartels into more numerous and more violent successors, principally Sinaloa and CJNG, which diversified into extortion, kidnapping, fuel theft, and human trafficking.

blocks.t: Estimates exceed 300,000 to 340,000 dead since 2006. More than 115,000 people are formally registered as missing, over ninety percent of them since 2006. Hundreds of thousands have been displaced. Cartels are estimated to control or contest roughly a third of Mexican territory.
This is what happens when drug money becomes larger than the state that is supposed to police it. The missing are the heart of it — 115,000 families who never got a body, a grave, or an answer.

de: Facing one of Europe's worst heroin epidemics, Portugal removed criminal penalties for personal possession of all drugs while keeping trafficking illegal, and redirected funding into treatment, housing, and employment support. Users are referred to health panels rather than courts.

blocks.t: Drug-related HIV infections and overdose deaths fell dramatically over the following decade and Portugal's overdose rate has remained among the lowest in Europe. Results have been more mixed since 2017 as funding was cut and drug use rose again in some cities.

Portugal is the clearest natural experiment available. What worked was not the decriminalization alone but the treatment investment paired with it — and when the funding was cut, the gains partly reversed.

de: Illicitly manufactured fentanyl, roughly fifty times more potent than heroin, entered the U.S. supply. Because it is synthetic it needs no farmland, no harvest, and no growing season, which made interdiction far harder. It is now pressed into counterfeit pills sold as oxycodone or Xanax.

blocks.t: U.S. overdose deaths peaked near 110,000 in 2022. Roughly 69 percent of all overdose deaths in 2023 involved synthetic opioids. Deaths among teenagers rose sharply, driven largely by counterfeit pills bought through social media.

Fentanyl broke the old model entirely. A lethal dose fits on a pencil tip and a child can order it on a phone. The single most important protective factor is a parent who knows what their child is doing online.

t: The First Real Decline in Decades
meta: A Response That Helped · United States
de: After twenty-five years of nearly uninterrupted increase, U.S. overdose deaths fell from about 110,000 in 2023 to roughly 80,000 in 2024 — a 27 percent drop, the largest single-year decline ever recorded. Provisional CDC data show a further fall to about 70,000 in 2025, a third consecutive year of decline. Researchers credit widespread naloxone distribution, expanded treatment access, and changes in the drug supply.

blocks.t: Opioid-involved deaths fell from roughly 83,000 in 2023 to about 45,000 in 2025. Nearly every state improved. Overdose nonetheless remains the leading cause of death for Americans aged 18 to 44, and deaths remain above pre-2019 levels.

End on this. The worst drug epidemic in American history is receding, and it is receding because people acted — naloxone in ordinary hands, treatment made reachable, families who did not give up. These problems are not fate. They respond to effort.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Ancient Egypt · Amarna, Egypt
de: Pharaoh Akhenaten abolished Egypt's traditional religion by decree, closed the temples, defunded the priesthoods, erased the name of Amun from monuments, and required worship of the Aten alone. It is the earliest well-documented attempt by a state to impose a single religion on an entire population by force.

blocks.t: The change did not survive him. Within a generation of his death the temples reopened, the old worship returned, and later pharaohs erased Akhenaten from the king lists and demolished his city.
The first recorded state religion imposed from above lasted less than one lifetime. Belief compelled by decree does not outlive the ruler who decreed it.

de: After conquering Babylon, Cyrus the Great permitted deported peoples to return home and rebuild their temples. The Cyrus Cylinder, now in the British Museum, records this policy. Ezra 1 records the decree permitting the Jewish people to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.

blocks.t: The Persian Empire became the largest the world had yet seen and governed diverse peoples with comparatively little religious revolt. The Second Temple was built. Isaiah had named Cyrus roughly 150 years earlier.

The first great empire to practice religious toleration as deliberate policy also became the most stable of its age. Heavenly Father used a Persian king who did not know Him to free His covenant people.

meta: Liberty Extended · Buddhist India · Mauryan Empire, India
de: Emperor Ashoka, after converting to Buddhism following a war he came to regret, carved edicts across his empire. Rock Edict XII instructs that one should honour the faith of others, that whoever exalts his own faith while disparaging another damages his own, and that concord among all faiths is good.

blocks.t: Mauryan India under Ashoka is remembered as one of the ancient world's most prosperous and least internally violent empires. Ashoka sent missionaries rather than armies, and Buddhism spread across Asia without conquest.
A Buddhist emperor with absolute power chose persuasion over compulsion in the third century BC. His faith spread further than religions that used the sword.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Hellenistic Greek · Jerusalem
de: The Seleucid king Antiochus IV banned Sabbath observance, circumcision, and possession of the Torah on pain of death, and desecrated the Temple in Jerusalem by installing pagan worship there.

blocks.t: The Maccabean revolt followed. Within three years the Temple was recaptured and rededicated, an event commemorated as Hanukkah. Seleucid control of Judea collapsed.
Suppressing a faith by law made it stronger and cost the empire the province. This pattern repeats across the whole layer.

t: The Hasmoneans Force Conversion of the Idumeans
meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Judaism · Idumea, south of Judea
de: After Jewish independence, the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus conquered Idumea and, according to Josephus, required the Idumean population to accept circumcision and Jewish law or leave the land.

blocks.t: The Idumeans were absorbed into the Jewish nation. A little over a century later, Herod the Great, of Idumean descent, ruled Judea as a client king of Rome and slaughtered the children of Bethlehem.

Included because integrity requires it. A people that had just been persecuted for its faith turned and imposed that faith on someone else within two generations. No tradition is exempt from this temptation.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Roman State Religion · Roman Empire
de: Beginning under Nero and recurring under Domitian, Decius, and Diocletian, Roman authorities required sacrifice to the emperor and the state gods. Christians who refused were imprisoned, enslaved, or executed. The Diocletianic persecution beginning in 303 was the most systematic.

blocks.t: Christianity grew throughout the persecution. By 313 it was legalized and within a century it was the empire's dominant faith. Tertullian famously observed that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.
Three centuries of the most powerful state on earth trying to suppress a faith produced the opposite of what was intended.

meta: Liberty Extended · Roman Empire · Milan, Italy
de: Constantine and Licinius agreed to grant to Christians and to all others free choice to follow the form of worship they wished, and restored confiscated property. It extended toleration to every religion in the empire, not to Christianity alone.

blocks.t: Persecution ended. Churches were built openly. Christian scholarship and charitable institutions expanded rapidly across the empire.
For sixty-seven years Rome practiced genuine religious liberty, and Christianity flourished under it. What happened next is the entry below.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Christianity · Constantinople and Rome
de: The Edict of Thessalonica in 380 made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the empire. By 392 Theodosius I had banned all pagan sacrifice and worship, closed temples, and ended the Olympic Games. Non-Nicene Christians were also suppressed.

blocks.t: Within eighty years of legalization, the persecuted had become the persecutors. Classical learning declined as temples and schools closed. In 415 the philosopher Hypatia was murdered by a mob in Alexandria.

This is the hinge of the entire layer. Christianity grew fastest when it was free and forbidden. It began to calcify the moment it gained the power to compel. Latter-day Saints understand this period as part of the Great Apostasy.

de: The agreement establishing the community at Medina included the Jewish tribes as a single community with the believers, granting them their religion and the Muslims theirs, with mutual defense obligations.

blocks.t: Medina became a functioning multi-religious polity. Early Islamic expansion generally permitted Jews and Christians to keep their faith as protected peoples subject to a tax, rather than requiring conversion.
Islam's founding document at Medina granted religious protection to a minority. Later Islamic states diverged widely from this, in both directions, as the entries below show.

t: Charlemagne Baptizes the Saxons by Force
meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Christianity · Saxony, Germany
de: Charlemagne's capitulary for Saxony imposed the death penalty for refusing baptism, for cremating the dead according to pagan custom, and for eating meat during Lent. At Verden in 782 the Royal Frankish Annals record the execution of 4,500 surrendered Saxon captives. Historians debate that figure — some judge it annalistic exaggeration, a later copying error, or a conflation of several events — but the episode as a mass execution of defeated Saxons is not seriously disputed.

blocks.t: Saxony was Christianized. Alcuin of York, Charlemagne's own leading scholar, criticised the mass beheadings in letters around 786 and argued that forced conversion was worthless because a person must come to Christ by free will.
Charlemagne's own chief advisor told him at the time that forced baptism does not make a Christian. The objection is not modern hindsight. It was raised in the room.

t: The Crusades and the Rhineland Massacres
meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Christianity · Rhineland, Europe and the Levant
de: Before the First Crusade reached the Holy Land, crusader bands massacred Jewish communities in Speyer, Worms, Mainz, and Cologne. Over two centuries the Crusades killed Muslims, Jews, and Eastern Christians. In 1204 crusaders sacked Constantinople, a Christian city.

blocks.t: The Crusades permanently damaged relations between Christianity, Islam, and Eastern Orthodoxy. The 1204 sack so weakened Constantinople that historians consider it a major cause of its fall to the Ottomans in 1453.
Wars fought in Christ's name contradicted nearly everything He taught. No prophet sanctioned these campaigns.

t: The Almohads Force Conversion in Spain and North Africa
meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Islam · Al-Andalus and the Maghreb
de: The Almohad dynasty abolished the protected status that had allowed Jews and Christians to practice their faiths under earlier Muslim rule in Spain and North Africa, and required conversion, exile, or death.

blocks.t: The Jewish community of Cordoba, one of the most learned in the world, was destroyed or scattered. The philosopher Maimonides fled as a child and eventually settled in Egypt. The centuries-long flourishing of Jewish scholarship under Muslim Spain ended.

The same civilization that had produced convivencia and preserved Greek philosophy for Europe also produced this. Traditions are not uniformly tolerant or intolerant across time. Policy is what changes.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Christianity · Spain
de: Established by the Catholic Monarchs with papal authorization, the Inquisition investigated the sincerity of converts from Judaism and Islam. Modern archival research indicates roughly 3,000 to 5,000 executions across its 356-year span, alongside far larger numbers of imprisonments, confiscations, and forced penances. Henry Kamen puts the maximum near 3,000; some scholars such as Andrea Del Col estimate substantially higher, up to about 12,000, because records from the intense early period before 1530 are poor. All modern figures are far below the 19th-century propaganda claims of tens of thousands.

blocks.t: Spain lost much of its merchant, medical, and scholarly class. Historians widely link the expulsion of Jews and Muslims and the climate of suspicion to Spain's long economic and intellectual decline relative to tolerant Protestant northern Europe.
Spain held the richest empire on earth and squandered the advantage by driving out the people who made its economy work. Enforced orthodoxy has a price, and it is usually paid in prosperity.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Christianity · Granada, Spain
de: Ferdinand and Isabella ordered every Jew in Spain to convert to Christianity or leave the country within four months. Estimates of those expelled range from 40,000 to 200,000. A decade later the same choice was imposed on Spanish Muslims.

blocks.t: Sephardic Jews scattered to the Ottoman Empire, North Africa, and the Netherlands. The Ottoman Sultan Bayezid II welcomed them, reportedly marveling that Ferdinand had impoverished his own kingdom and enriched Ottoman lands. Amsterdam, which received many, became a center of European finance.
One nation expelled its minority and declined. The nations that received them prospered. The experiment ran side by side in the same century.

t: State Religion and Human Sacrifice in the Aztec Empire
meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Aztec State Religion · Tenochtitlan, Mexico
de: The Aztec state required tribute in captives for ritual sacrifice at the Templo Mayor. Subject peoples were obligated to supply victims. Estimates of annual sacrifices vary widely among historians, but archaeological excavation of the skull rack at the Templo Mayor has confirmed the practice at scale.

blocks.t: Resentment among subject peoples was so deep that tens of thousands of Tlaxcalans and others allied with Cortes against Tenochtitlan. The empire was brought down substantially by its own tributary nations.
A state religion that demanded its subjects supply victims created the alliance that destroyed it. Included so that this layer does not treat coercion as a European or Middle Eastern phenomenon.

de: The Peace of Augsburg ended fighting between Lutheran and Catholic states with the principle cuius regio, eius religio, meaning the ruler of each territory determined its religion. Subjects who disagreed were permitted to emigrate rather than convert.

blocks.t: It stopped a war and established a limited right of exit, but it made belief a function of geography. Anabaptists and Reformed Christians were excluded from its protection entirely and continued to be persecuted by Lutherans and Catholics alike.
A genuine step forward and still not freedom. The right to leave is not the same as the right to believe.

de: Meeting during the interregnum after the last Jagiellonian king died, the Polish-Lithuanian Sejm swore to keep peace among those differing in faith and not to shed blood on account of religion. The parchment carries 206 wax seals and was entered in the UNESCO Memory of the World Register in 2003. An honest limit: it guaranteed liberty to the nobility and free persons, not to peasants, so it was not religious freedom in the modern universal sense.

blocks.t: Poland-Lithuania became a refuge for Jews, Anabaptists, Antitrinitarians and Orthodox Christians while the rest of Europe burned. Cardinal Hozjusz complained that the country had become a place of shelter for heretics. Every newly elected king was required to swear to uphold the act at his coronation, and the historian Norman Davies judges that it governed religious life in the Republic for over two hundred years.
While western Europe fought religious wars, the largest state in Europe chose toleration and drew in the people other nations drove out.

t: The Edict of Nantes and Its Revocation
de: Henry IV granted French Protestants substantial rights of worship, ending decades of religious war that had included the Saint Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572. In 1685 Louis XIV revoked it, ordering Protestant churches demolished and emigration forbidden.

blocks.t: Despite the ban, an estimated 200,000 to 400,000 Huguenots fled to England, the Netherlands, Prussia, and America, taking with them skills in textiles, watchmaking, and finance. Prussia and England gained industries. France lost them.
France ran the experiment in both directions within a century. Toleration brought peace and prosperity. Revocation exported both to its rivals.

meta: Liberty Extended · Christianity · Providence, Rhode Island
de: Banished from Massachusetts Bay for arguing that civil authority has no jurisdiction over conscience, Roger Williams founded Providence with liberty of conscience for all, including Jews, Quakers, and those of no faith, and argued for a wall of separation between the garden of the church and the wilderness of the world.

blocks.t: Rhode Island received the first Jewish congregation in North America and became a haven for Baptists and Quakers persecuted elsewhere in New England. Its charter language influenced later American guarantees.
The idea that government has no authority over the soul was first put into practice in America by a Puritan minister the Puritans threw out.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Christianity · Salem, Massachusetts
de: Massachusetts Bay authorities executed twenty people and imprisoned about 150 more on charges of witchcraft, relying heavily on spectral evidence. The colony later reversed the convictions and issued a public day of fasting and repentance.

blocks.t: Salem became a permanent cautionary example in American law and culture, contributing to the conviction that the state must not adjudicate the invisible.
The colony that expelled Roger Williams for defending conscience hanged twenty of its own neighbors within a lifetime. Communities that will not tolerate dissent eventually turn on themselves.

meta: Liberty Extended · United States · Philadelphia and the United States
de: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof. Preceded by Virginia's 1786 Statute for Religious Freedom, drafted by Jefferson and carried by Madison, which held that no man shall be compelled to frequent or support any religious worship.

blocks.t: The United States became the first major nation founded without an established church. It produced neither the religious collapse its critics predicted nor the theocracy its critics feared, and sustained unusually high rates of both religious practice and religious diversity.
D&C 101:80 identifies the Constitution's framers as wise men raised up by Heavenly Father for this purpose. Without the First Amendment there is no legal space for the Restoration.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Anti-Mormon persecution · Missouri, USA
de: Governor Lilburn Boggs issued Missouri Executive Order 44, stating that the Mormons must be treated as enemies and must be exterminated or driven from the state. Three days later at Hawn's Mill, a militia force killed seventeen Latter-day Saints, including a ten-year-old boy. The Saints were expelled from Missouri in winter.

blocks.t: The Saints fled to Illinois, were driven out again after Joseph Smith's murder in 1844, and crossed the plains to the Salt Lake Valley. The order was not formally rescinded until 1976.
Religious persecution in America is not a foreign or a distant story. It was carried out by a state government against Latter-day Saints, and the First Amendment did not prevent it.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Latter-day Saints · Mountain Meadows, Utah
de: During a period of war hysteria in Utah Territory, a local militia of Latter-day Saints, with some Paiute participation, attacked and then massacred approximately 120 emigrants of the Baker-Fancher party traveling from Arkansas to California, sparing only seventeen children under the age of seven.

blocks.t: John D. Lee was convicted and executed in 1877. The Church has since acknowledged the massacre publicly. In 2007 Elder Henry B. Eyring, speaking for the Church at the site, expressed profound regret and stated that the Church's local leaders and members bore responsibility.

Included because this layer would be worthless without it. A people who had themselves been driven out by an extermination order committed a massacre nineteen years later. The lesson of this entire layer is not that some faiths are dangerous and ours is safe. It is that certainty plus fear plus power is dangerous in anyone's hands, including our own.

meta: Belief Suppressed by the State · State Atheism - Soviet · Soviet Union
de: The Soviet state confiscated church property, executed and imprisoned clergy of every faith, dynamited cathedrals including Christ the Saviour in Moscow in 1931, established the League of the Militant Godless, and taught atheism as compulsory curriculum. Orthodox Christians, Catholics, Jews, Muslims, and Buddhists were all targeted.

blocks.t: Tens of thousands of clergy were killed. Of roughly 54,000 Orthodox churches open in 1917, a few hundred remained functioning by 1939. Belief persisted underground. When restrictions lifted after 1991, religious practice revived rapidly across the former Soviet bloc.

The largest and most sustained attempt in history to abolish religion by state power failed. Seventy years of compulsory atheism did not extinguish faith. It only drove it into kitchens and basements.

t: The Saudi State and Enforced Religion
meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Islam - Wahhabi · Saudi Arabia
de: The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was founded on an alliance between the House of Saud and Wahhabi religious authority. Public non-Muslim worship is prohibited, conversion from Islam is treated as apostasy, and religious police long enforced observance. Pew has repeatedly ranked Saudi Arabia among the world's most restrictive states on religion.

blocks.t: Saudi oil wealth funded the export of Wahhabi religious institutions worldwide for decades. Some reforms have occurred since 2017, but non-Muslim public worship remains prohibited and apostasy remains a capital offense in law.

Enormous natural wealth has not produced the intellectual or scientific output of far poorer but freer societies. Money can buy universities. It cannot buy the freedom to question, which is what makes them work.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Nazi Germany · Germany and occupied Europe
de: The Nazi state stripped Jews of citizenship, then property, then life, murdering approximately six million Jewish people along with Roma, disabled people, Jehovah's Witnesses, and others. Churches were pressured into compliance; those who resisted, such as Dietrich Bonhoeffer, were executed.

blocks.t: European Jewish civilization was largely destroyed. The scale of the crime directly produced the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the modern international framework of religious liberty protection.

The most industrially advanced and best-educated nation in Europe carried this out. Education and technology are not moral safeguards. Only conscience is, and conscience requires the freedom to refuse.

meta: Liberty Extended · United Nations · Paris, France
de: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirmed that everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including the freedom to change religion or belief and to manifest it in teaching, practice, worship and observance.

blocks.t: Article 18 became the standard against which religious restriction is now measured worldwide, and the basis for Pew's Government Restrictions Index and the work of the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom.
The right to change your religion is the hinge of the whole article. A faith you may not leave is not a faith you have chosen.

meta: Liberty Extended · Roman Catholic · Vatican City
de: The Second Vatican Council declared that the human person has a right to religious freedom, that no one is to be forced to act against his convictions in religious matters, and that this right is founded on the dignity of the person as known through revealed truth and reason.

blocks.t: The Church that had authorized the Inquisition formally repudiated religious coercion. Pope John Paul II later issued public apologies for historical wrongs committed in the Church's name.
Institutions can repent. The tradition that produced some of the worst entries on this layer produced one of the clearest defenses of conscience in the twentieth century.

t: The World's First Officially Atheist State
meta: Belief Suppressed by the State · State Atheism - Albania · Albania
de: Following a speech by Enver Hoxha on February 6, 1967, Albania became the world's first constitutionally atheist state. Records compiled by the Albanian Institute of Political Studies count 2,169 religious institutions closed — 740 mosques, 608 Orthodox churches, 157 Catholic churches, and 530 Sufi and Bektashi sites. Buildings were demolished or repurposed; the cathedral at Shkoder became a sports arena. Clergy were imprisoned or executed, and the 1976 constitution declared that the State recognises no religion and supports atheistic propaganda.

blocks.t: Albania became the poorest and most isolated country in Europe. When enforcement ended in late 1990, Father Simon Jubani — newly released from political prison — celebrated the first public Mass since 1967 in a Shkoder cemetery on November 4. Contemporary accounts put the crowd at a later November Mass near 50,000. Albania today is noted for unusually peaceful relations among Muslims, Orthodox, and Catholics.
The most complete abolition of religion ever attempted produced neither prosperity nor progress, only isolation and poverty. Faith returned within a single year of being permitted.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Islam - Shia · Iran
de: The revolution established clerical rule with religious law enforced by the state. Bahai adherents face systematic exclusion from higher education and employment; conversion from Islam is treated as apostasy; morality police enforce dress and conduct. Pew consistently ranks Iran among the most restrictive countries on religion.

blocks.t: Iran has experienced sustained emigration of educated professionals and, according to independent surveys, a marked rise in religious disaffiliation among younger Iranians raised under compulsory religion.

Compulsory religion appears to produce the sharpest decline in sincere belief. Iranian young people raised under enforced faith are among the most secular in the region. Force does not make believers. It makes performers, and eventually it makes skeptics.

t: The Taliban and the Bamiyan Buddhas
meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Islam - Taliban · Afghanistan
de: The Taliban banned education for girls, enforced dress and worship by decree, persecuted the Shia Hazara minority, and in March 2001 dynamited the sixth-century Bamiyan Buddha statues despite international appeals, including from Muslim governments.

blocks.t: Afghanistan ranks among the world's lowest in literacy, life expectancy, and economic output. Since the 2021 return to power, girls have again been barred from secondary and higher education.
A country that forbids half its children to learn has decided its future. There is no example in history of a society that suppressed the education of women and then prospered.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Islam - ISIS · Iraq and Syria
de: ISIS declared a caliphate and gave Christians and other minorities the choice of conversion, a tax, or death. Against the Yazidis it went further: men were massacred and thousands of women and girls were enslaved. The United Nations, the U.S. Congress, and the European Parliament formally recognized this as genocide.

blocks.t: The territorial caliphate was destroyed by 2019 after drawing a global military coalition. Ancient Christian and Yazidi communities in the Nineveh Plains, present for well over a thousand years, were largely emptied.
The most explicitly theocratic state of the modern era lasted five years and was destroyed by an alliance that included many Muslim nations. Muslims were also its most numerous victims.

meta: Faith Imposed by Force · Buddhist nationalism · Rakhine State, Myanmar
de: Myanmar security forces, supported by Buddhist nationalist movements, conducted operations against the Rohingya Muslim minority. More than 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. The UN fact-finding mission described the actions as carrying genocidal intent, and the case is before the International Court of Justice.

blocks.t: One of the world's largest refugee populations. Myanmar has faced sanctions and international isolation, and returned to civil war after a 2021 coup.
Included because Buddhism is popularly imagined in the West as incapable of this. No tradition is immune when religion fuses with national identity and state power.

t: The Uyghur Camps and the Sinicization of Religion
meta: Belief Suppressed by the State · State Atheism - China · Xinjiang, China
de: China has detained large numbers of Uyghur Muslims in extrajudicial camps, demolished and altered mosques, restricted fasting and religious instruction, and required religions to be sinicized. Churches have been closed and crosses removed; Tibetan Buddhist practice and Falun Gong are also restricted. Pew ranks China at or near the top of its Government Restrictions Index.

blocks.t: Multiple governments have designated the treatment of Uyghurs as genocide or crimes against humanity. A 2022 UN human rights report found possible crimes against humanity. Underground Christian congregations in China have continued to grow.
The largest current program of religious control on earth is run by an officially atheist state. Coercion is not a religious impulse. It is a power impulse, and it uses whatever creed is at hand.

de: Pew Research Center measures religious restriction across 198 countries on two indexes. In its most recent reporting, 58 countries had high or very high government restrictions on religion, just below the record 59 set the previous year. Countries with very high government restrictions included China, Iran, Afghanistan, Indonesia, Syria, and Uzbekistan. Countries with very high social hostilities included Nigeria, India, Israel, Syria, Bangladesh, and Pakistan. The United States scored low on government restrictions.

blocks.t: Pew has also found that among countries with high or very high government restrictions, more than two-thirds are classified as authoritarian, most give preferential treatment to a favored religion, and none are classified as full democracies.
Not a single full democracy appears among the world's most religiously restrictive states. Religious freedom and political freedom rise and fall together.

meta: Liberty Extended · Economic research · Cross-national research
de: Brian Grim of Georgetown, with Greg Clark and Robert Snyder of Brigham Young University, tested religious freedom against the World Economic Forum's Global Competitiveness Index. They found a positive relationship with ten of the twelve pillars of global competitiveness, and found government restrictions on religion and social hostilities to be detrimental to economic growth while controlling for twenty-three other economic, political, social, and demographic variables.

blocks.t: The finding has been cited by the U.S. State Department and the World Economic Forum. Separate research by Grim estimates religion's annual contribution to the U.S. economy at roughly 1.2 trillion dollars through congregations, charities, schools, and faith-based businesses.

An honest caution: this is strong correlation with controls, not a settled proof of causation. Wealthy stable countries may find toleration easier to afford. What the data does show clearly is that no nation has ever restricted religion its way to prosperity.

t: Honour Thy Father and Thy Mother
de: Among the Ten Commandments given at Sinai, the fifth is the only one that comes with a promise attached: honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land. Israelite law went on to codify inheritance, betrothal, the protection of widows and orphans, and the care of the poor. The family became a legal and covenantal unit, not merely a household arrangement.

blocks.t: The Jewish people have survived exile, dispersion across every continent, centuries of persecution, and attempted extermination — without a homeland for 1,900 years. The household, not the state, carried the identity.
A people can lose its land, its temple, and its language and still survive, if the family keeps the covenant. Heavenly Father built His people to be portable.

de: Under the agoge, Spartan boys were removed from their homes at age seven and raised by the state in barracks until age thirty. Marriage existed but husbands lived apart from wives for years.
